855.title: A threefold cord (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
855.hook: two are better than one, and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken"
855.carry: woe to him that is alone
855.howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is studied in Jewish teaching on friendship and community, and some readers take the third strand as God between two people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's poem of pairs: to every thing there is a season. Your line was a time for everything. What season did you name for yourself? Today, Kohelet stops looking at time and looks at the people beside us. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Pull a single thread from the hem of a shirt and snap it between your fingers. Easy. Now take three threads, twist them together, and try again. It bites into your skin. It holds. The strength isn't in one heroic strand. It's in ordinary strands wound around each other. Kohelet, the man who called everything breath, noticed the same thing about people. Today, a few verses about not being alone.
screen: `ONE THREAD SNAPS.` → `THREE THREADS, TWISTED, HOLD.` → `NOT BEING ALONE.`

segments.voice: Just before this passage, Kohelet describes a man who is entirely alone. No child, no brother, and yet there is no end to his work, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches. He never stops to ask who he is laboring for. That is hevel, Kohelet says. Breath. And then he turns, in the words of the King James text: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Then three small pictures. The first: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." A stumble on a road, and a hand reaching down. The second: if two lie together, they have heat, but how can one be warm alone? A cold night, and the warmth of someone near. The third: if one is attacked, two can stand against the attacker. Then the last line, the one that stays: "a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Wait. He's been talking about two. Where does the third strand come from? Readers have offered more than one answer. Some say it's a way of saying: if two are strong, three are stronger still. Some see the third strand as God, woven between two people. Others see a community, the friend of a friend, the circle that holds a pair together. The text leaves the third strand unnamed. Notice, too, the word quickly. Not never broken. A cord can still fray. But wound together, it takes longer, and it gives time for someone to come and help. A threefold cord.
screen: `THE MAN WHO WORKS ALONE.` · `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.` · `LIFTED, WARMED, DEFENDED.` · then, large: `A THREEFOLD CORD IS NOT QUICKLY BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to strengthen one friendship. Bring to mind one person you care about but haven't really talked to in a while. Picture where they might be right now, what their day looks like. Then think of one small thread you could add today: a message, a call, a question about something they care about, a memory you share. Just choose it; you'll send it after the bell. If you pray, you can pray for that friend by name. If not, hold their name gently while the time passes. The bell holds the time.
Threefold cord. Ecclesiastes four: two are better than one, and a cord of three strands, twisted together, is not quickly broken. Today's word.
Your line: woe to him that is alone. Today, send that one message to the friend you chose, and if you can, bring a third person into the thread. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Eat thy bread with joy (Ecclesiastes 9:7–10)
856.hook: enjoy your life, and do what your hand finds to do with all your might
856.howItsDone: Before eating bread, Jews say a blessing, hamotzi, thanking God who brings forth bread from the earth, and after the meal they say a grace, Birkat Hamazon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two are better than one, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Your line was woe to him that is alone. Did a message go out to an old friend? Today, Kohelet, of all people, tells us to enjoy our food. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

Lunch, eaten standing up. One hand holds the sandwich, the other scrolls. Somewhere around the fourth bite the sandwich is gone, and there's no memory of how it tasted. The mind was three meetings ahead the whole time. Now listen to who is about to talk about this. Kohelet. The man who said all is breath. The one who watched the wise die like the foolish. You might expect him to say food doesn't matter either. He says the opposite.
screen: `LUNCH, EATEN STANDING UP.` → `NO MEMORY OF THE TASTE.` → `KOHELET SAYS THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes nine, in the words of the King James text: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works." Go thy way. It sounds almost like a dismissal: stop worrying, go and eat. And look at the reason Kohelet gives. Not because you've earned it. Because God now accepteth thy works. In his telling, the meal isn't a reward to be won later. The acceptance has come first. Then Kohelet keeps going, piling up ordinary gifts. Let your clothes be white, and your head not lack oil: dress for a good day. Live joyfully with the wife you love, all the days of your fleeting life. The Hebrew for those days is the word from a few days ago, hevel. Breath. And that's the turn. Kohelet doesn't say enjoy life because it lasts. He says enjoy it because it doesn't. Breath is short, so taste the bread. Then the verse that gives the joy some muscle: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest." That's a sobering reason, and Kohelet gives it straight. The work in front of you is yours now, not later. So this isn't a call to idle pleasure. It's two halves of one way of living: eat with joy, and work with your whole strength. Be present at the table, and present at the task. Some readers hear these lines as the quiet heart of the whole book, the place where its doubt and its gladness meet. Eat thy bread with joy.

segments.voice: Today's practice is to enjoy one meal fully, and to rehearse it now. Think of the next thing you'll eat. Picture it in front of you: the color, the smell, the first bite. Imagine eating it sitting down, phone out of reach, chewing slowly enough to taste it. Then picture the moment after, when you stand up and turn to whatever your hand finds to do. Jewish practice sets a blessing before eating; if you pray, you can say the one you know. If not, a moment of thanks is enough. The bell holds the time.
Kohelet, the voice of Ecclesiastes, who says life is breath, so eat your bread with joy and work with all your might. Today's word.
Your line: do it with thy might. Today, eat one meal sitting down, slowly, and then give one task your whole strength. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: Cast thy bread (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
857.hook: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days"
857.carry: thou knowest not which shall prosper
857.howItsDone: Some Jewish commentators read Ecclesiastes 11:1 as a teaching about kindness and tzedakah given with no promise of return; in some communities the book of Ecclesiastes is read aloud in synagogue on Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet told us to eat our bread with joy and do whatever our hands find to do. Your line was do it with thy might. Did one meal get your full attention? Today, the same book takes the bread out of your hands and sends it down a river. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

Bread, tossed from a riverbank onto moving water. It floats for a second, turns, and the current takes it. By any normal reckoning, that bread is gone. Nobody gets a receipt from a river. And yet near the end of Ecclesiastes, the book that kept saying all is breath, comes this odd instruction: "Cast thy bread upon the waters, For thou shalt find it after many days." Let it go, says the teacher, and it will come back to you. Today's word is that strange advice.
screen: `BREAD ON MOVING WATER.` → `NO RECEIPT FROM A RIVER.` → `IT WILL COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Cast thy bread. The verse never says how the bread comes back, or when, beyond after many days. So readers have filled the gap in different ways. Some hear a merchant's advice: send your goods out across the sea, and the profit returns in time. Some hear charity: give to people who can never repay you, and the good finds its way home. The commentator Rashi reads it as kindness done for someone you expect never to see again. The next verse keeps the hand open: "Divide a portion into seven, yea, even into eight; For thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth." Not one gift, carefully placed. Seven shares, and then one more. Then Kohelet turns to the person who waits for perfect conditions: "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; And he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap." If you stand in the field checking the sky, the seed stays in the bag. And then the line that ties it together: "In the morning sow thy seed, And in the evening withhold not thy hand; For thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that." Notice what the teacher does not promise. He doesn't say every gift returns. He says you don't know. That not-knowing, which earlier in the book made everything feel like breath, becomes here the reason to keep giving. If you can't tell which seed will grow, sow in the morning and again in the evening. If you can't tell which kindness will matter, offer more than one. The bread on the water is not an investment with a guaranteed return. It's a gift, let go.
screen: `HOW IT COMES BACK IS NEVER SAID.` · `SEVEN, YEA, EVEN EIGHT.` · then, large: `WHO WATCHES THE WIND WON'T SOW.` · then: `YOU DON'T KNOW, SO KEEP GIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without a guarantee. Sit back for a moment. Let one small gift come to mind that you could offer today with no way to know where it lands: a kind word to a stranger, a donation no one will thank you for, an honest compliment to someone you may never see again. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold bread before you toss it. Then decide that you'll let it go, and not stand at the bank watching the water afterward. If you pray, you can offer the gift with a word of prayer as it goes. The bell holds the time.
Sow. Ecclesiastes' advice to give and let go, casting your bread and sowing your seed before you know what will grow. Today's word.
Your line: thou knowest not which shall prosper. Today, give one thing away without keeping track of whether it comes back. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: The holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5)
858.hook: Rabbi Akiva called the Song of Songs the holy of holies among the writings
858.tomorrow: I am my beloved's (Song of Songs 6:3)
858.howItsDone: In Ashkenazi custom the Song of Songs is read in synagogue during Passover, and in some communities it is recited on Friday evening before the Sabbath begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet told us to send our bread out on the water and stop waiting for perfect weather. Your line was thou knowest not which shall prosper. What did you let go of? Today, a love song, and a rabbi who called it holy. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

Why is a book of love poetry in the Bible at all? Open the Song of Songs and you'll find kisses, a garden, a lover leaping over the hills like a gazelle, a woman searching the city streets at night for the one she loves. No laws. No kings at war. No prophets thundering. The rabbis of the Mishnah asked a version of that question out loud, and one of them answered it with startling praise. Today's word is the book's own name.
screen: `A BOOK OF LOVE POETRY.` → `NO LAWS, NO KINGS AT WAR.` → `WHY IS IT HERE?`

segments.voice: Shir HaShirim. The Song of Songs. Hebrew can say the best of something by doubling a word. The holy of holies is the holiest place, and the song of songs, by the same pattern, is a song above songs. The book's first verse names it: "The song of songs, which is Solomon's." In the Mishnah, tractate Yadayim, the rabbis discuss which books are holy scripture. Their way of putting it is unusual: a holy scroll is one that makes the hands impure, so you wash after handling it. Some there said the Song of Songs was in dispute. Rabbi Akiva would have none of it. In the Mishnah's telling he says, in effect: heaven forbid. No one in Israel ever doubted the Song. The whole world was not as worthy as the day it was given to Israel. All the writings are holy, he says, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. Why say that about a love poem? Rabbinic midrash, such as Song of Songs Rabbah, reads the Song as a picture of the love between God and the people of Israel: the lover is God, the beloved is the people, and the searching and finding are their story together. Other readers hear it first as human love, and see no need to choose between the two. Rabbi Akiva's phrase can hold both: a song so close to the heart that it belongs in the innermost room. The Song even keeps a calendar. In its second chapter it says, "For, lo, the winter is past, The rain is over and gone," and it is read in synagogue in the spring, at Passover. Holy of holies, and also: love letters.
screen: `SONG OF SONGS: A SONG ABOVE SONGS.` · `SCROLLS THAT MAKE THE HANDS IMPURE.` · then, large: `THE SONG IS THE HOLY OF HOLIES.` · then: `GOD AND ISRAEL, AND HUMAN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse of the Song. If you have a Bible or a reading app nearby, open the Song of Songs anywhere, choose one verse, and read it slowly, twice. If not, take the line from the second chapter: the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Let it sit. Ask what kind of love it might be describing: between two people, between God and a people, or both. You don't have to decide. If you pray, you can read the verse as slowly as you would a prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shir HaShirim. The Song of Songs: a love poem that Rabbi Akiva called the holy of holies. Today's word.
Your line: a song above songs. Today, notice one ordinary tender thing, a note left on a table, a hand on a shoulder, and give it a moment of reverence. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: I am my beloved's (Song of Songs 6:3)
859.hook: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine"; tradition hears the month of Elul in its first letters
859.howItsDone: The verse 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine' is taught as a hint to the name of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, when Ashkenazi communities sound the shofar on weekday mornings and add Psalm 27 to the prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Akiva called a love poem the holy of holies. Your line was a song above songs. Did you find one tender, ordinary thing? Today, one line from inside that poem. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Four Hebrew letters: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. Put together, they spell Elul, the name of the month that comes just before Rosh Hashanah. Tradition says that month is hiding inside one line of the Song of Songs. Take the first letter of each of the line's first four Hebrew words, set them side by side, and there it is. A love song, carrying the name of a month on the calendar. Today's word is that line.
screen: `ALEPH, LAMED, VAV, LAMED.` → `ELUL, THE MONTH BEFORE ROSH HASHANAH.` → `HIDDEN IN ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: I am my beloved's. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, That feedeth among the lilies." In Hebrew: ani l'dodi v'dodi li. Ani, I. L'dodi, to my beloved. V'dodi, and my beloved. Li, to me. Aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. Elul. Earlier in the Song, nearly the same words come in the other order: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Some readers notice the turn. First she says he is hers. Later she begins with herself, given to him. Love that starts with having becomes love that starts with giving. Why tie the line to Elul? Elul is the month of getting ready for the High Holy Days. In Ashkenazi custom the shofar is sounded on weekday mornings through the month, until the day before Rosh Hashanah, and Psalm twenty-seven is added to the daily prayers. It's a month for looking back, setting things right with people, and turning. The teaching about the letters, which comes from later Jewish writers, says this turning doesn't have to be a grim inspection. It can be two who love each other walking back toward each other. Read that way, the people say the first half to God, I am my beloved's, and God's answer is folded into the same sentence: and my beloved is mine. The line has another life too. Some couples engrave it inside wedding rings or speak it under the wedding canopy. The same four words carry a marriage and a month of return. One sentence, and it goes both ways.
screen: `ANI L'DODI V'DODI LI.` · `FIRST HE IS MINE, THEN I AM HIS.` · then, large: `ELUL: A MONTH OF TURNING BACK.` · then: `A COUPLE, AND A PEOPLE AND GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it to someone you love. Close your eyes if you like. Let one person come to mind: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend who has stayed. Hold them there for a moment. Then think of one way you are theirs: something you give, a way you show up. And one way they are yours. If they're nearby, or a message away, you might tell them today, in your own words. If you pray, you can say the verse itself, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Dodi. My beloved: from the Song of Songs' line ani l'dodi v'dodi li, whose first letters spell Elul. Today's word.
Your line: love that starts with giving. Today, give one person you love a sign that you're theirs: a call, a note, ten minutes of full attention. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6–7)
860.hook: "love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench love"
860.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the Song of Songs as love between God and Israel as well as between people, and some couples use the words 'set me as a seal upon thy heart' at their weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four Hebrew words whose first letters spell Elul. Your line was love that starts with giving. Who did you tell? Today, near its last page, the Song makes a bold claim about love. Day eight hundred sixty.

"Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it." Floods are an old picture of a force nothing stops. In Genesis the waters rise until the mountains are covered. Here, close to the end of the Song of Songs, the waters meet something they can't put out. The woman in the Song asks her beloved to keep her close, and then she tells him why: because love holds on as hard as the one thing nobody escapes. Today's word is that comparison.
screen: `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` → `A FIRE THE FLOODS CAN'T PUT OUT.` → `AS STRONG AS WHAT NOBODY ESCAPES.`

segments.voice: Strong as death. Here's the verse that comes first, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD." A seal is a mark that says whose something is. Set me as a seal means: wear me where you can't forget me, on your heart and on your arm. In Hebrew the line runs azzah khamavet ahavah: strong as death, love. Death doesn't give back what it takes. The Song says love holds on just as hard. Not gentler than death. Equal to it. Then the flame. The verse's last word in Hebrew is shalhevetyah, and its last syllable, yah, is also a short form of God's name. The JPS translators heard it that way: a very flame of the LORD. Others take the yah as a way of saying a mighty flame. The text lets it flicker both ways. Then the floods. Water puts out fire. That's what water does. Except this fire. And the verse closes with a warning: "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned." Love can't be bought. It can only be kept burning. And notice what the Song does not claim. It doesn't call love gentle, or easy, or safe; in the same breath it says jealousy is cruel as the grave. It calls love strong.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL UPON THY HEART.` · `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.` · then, large: `A FLAME CALLED SHALHEVETYAH.` · then: `LOVE CAN'T BE BOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set a seal. Bring to mind a love that has been tested: by distance, by time, by a hard season, maybe by a death. It might be someone still here, or someone you still love who is gone. Rest a hand on your heart, the place the Song asks to be worn like a seal. Hold that person there for a few slow breaths. Don't ask anything of the memory. Just let it be pressed in, the way a seal leaves its mark in wax. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
Azzah. Hebrew for strong: the Song's claim that love holds on as hard as death does, and many waters cannot quench it. Today's word.
Your line: many waters cannot quench it. Today, when a love asks something of you, patience, a drive, an apology, give it without counting what it costs. Day eight hundred sixty.

861.title: How doth the city sit (Lamentations 1:1)
861.hook: the city once full of people sits solitary, like a widow
861.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, the fast for the destruction of the Temples, Lamentations is chanted in synagogue in a mournful melody while people sit on the floor or on low stools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs said love is strong as death, and floods can't put it out. Your line was many waters cannot quench it. What did you feed? This week ran from a threefold cord, to bread cast on the water, to the Song's holy of holies. Today, a different kind of song. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A city, drawn as a woman, sitting on the ground. The streets around her used to be loud with people. Now nobody comes. That's the opening picture of the book of Lamentations, and it begins with one sighing word, eichah, how. Earlier on this path we heard that word chanted on Tisha B'Av, the fast for the Temples. Today we stay with the picture that follows it. Today's word is the whole first line.

segments.voice: How doth the city sit. The first verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "How doth the city sit solitary, That was full of people! How is she become as a widow! She that was great among the nations, And princess among the provinces, How is she become tributary!" Three pictures, one after another. Full of people, now alone. A wife, now a widow. A princess, now paying tribute to others. Each is a fall from a height, and each one is about a person, not a pile of stones. Lamentations doesn't describe the ruins of Jerusalem like a report. It turns the city into someone you could sit beside. Then it shows her at night: "She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers." Tears on her cheeks. Not falling, just there, the way tears stay when no one has come to wipe them. The chapter keeps coming back to those words: none to comfort her. Here's what the book does with all that. It doesn't argue. It doesn't hurry to explain why it happened, or how it will be fixed. It sits. Eichah is not a question waiting for an answer. It's a cry. And the city's posture becomes the posture of the people who read it: on Tisha B'Av, mourners sit low, on the floor or on low stools, while the book is chanted. Sometimes the honest thing a text can do is refuse to stand up too fast. How doth the city sit. Alone. And now someone is sitting with her: the one reading.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit for a minute in an empty room. If you can, find a room with no one else in it, or turn away from the screens around you. Sit down. Notice the quiet, and what's missing from it: voices, footsteps, someone who used to be there. Don't fill it. Just keep it company. If a loss comes to mind, yours or the world's, let it sit beside you. If you pray, you can let the silence be part of your prayer. The bell holds the time.
